claim: A connectome of the brain of a Drosophila melanogaster larva was recently mapped.
source: Recently, authors mapped a connectome of the brain of a D. melanogaster larva (Winding et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Winding et al., 2023.

claim: The larval Drosophila brain connectome was imaged using electron microscopy.
source: To understand how the neurons in this brain were connected to each other, the authors first imaged this brain using electron microscopy (Ohyama et al., 2015), and then manually reconstructed each neuron and its pre- and post-synaptic contacts.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ohyama et al., 2015.

claim: The larval Drosophila brain connectome consists of 3016 neurons and over 548,000 synapses.
source: This synaptic wiring diagram consists of 3016 neurons and over 548,000 synapses.
evidence: The claim provides specific numerical data about the connectome.

claim: The larval Drosophila brain connectome includes a complete reconstruction of both the left and right hemispheres.
source: Importantly, this work yielded a complete reconstruction of both the left and right hemispheres of the brain.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the connectome reconstruction.

claim: The left hemisphere network contains 1506 neurons.
source: This process yielded a 1506 neuron network for the left hemisphere, and a 1506 neuron network for the right (note that the number of nodes in the two hemispheres need not have been exactly the same).
evidence: The claim provides specific numerical data about the network construction.

claim: The right hemisphere network contains 1506 neurons.
source: This process yielded a 1506 neuron network for the left hemisphere, and a 1506 neuron network for the right (note that the number of nodes in the two hemispheres need not have been exactly the same).
evidence: The claim provides specific numerical data about the network construction.

claim: The density of the left hemisphere is approximately 0.93 times that of the right hemisphere.
source: this makes the left density ~0.93 that of the right.
evidence: The claim is based on a calculation from the observed densities shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The extremely small p-value for the density test resulted from the large sample size for this comparison.
source: While the ratio of the estimated densities is only ~0.93, this extremely small p-value resulted from the large sample size for this comparison, as there are 2,266,530 potential edges on both the left and the right sides.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the statistical properties of the test and the data.

claim: There are 2,266,530 potential edges on both the left and the right sides of the network.
source: While the ratio of the estimated densities is only ~0.93, this extremely small p-value resulted from the large sample size for this comparison, as there are 2,266,530 potential edges on both the left and the right sides.
evidence: The claim provides specific numerical data calculated from the network structure.

claim: For all the group-to-group connection probabilities which are different, the probability on the right hemisphere is higher.
source: Interestingly, for all the group-to-group connection probabilities which are different, the probability on the right hemisphere (which has the greater density) is higher (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: After density adjustment, two group-to-group connections are significantly different: KC → convergence neurons (CN) and KC → mushroom body output neurons (MBON).
source: After correction for multiple comparisons, there are two group-to-group connections which are significantly different (at significance level 0.05): KC → convergence neurons (CN) and KC → mushroom body output neurons (MBON).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical test results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: All significant differences between the hemispheres under the density-adjusted SBM are associated with the Kenyon cells.
source: Thus, all significant differences between the hemispheres under this version of the SBM are associated with the Kenyon cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the statistical test results.

claim: When Kenyon cells are excluded, the density-adjusted group connection test yields a p-value of approximately 0.60.
source: However, for the density-adjusted group connection test, the p-value was ~0.60, indicating that we no longer rejected bilateral symmetry under this definition when the Kenyon cells are excluded from the analysis (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical test results shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The difference between the left and right hemispheres can be explained as the combination of a global effect (the difference in density) and a cell type-specific effect (the difference in Kenyon cell projection probabilities).
source: This sequence of results suggests that the difference between the left and right hemispheres (at least in terms of the high-level network statistics studied here) can be explained as the combination of a global effect (the difference in density) and a cell type-specific effect (the difference in Kenyon cell projection probabilities).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined results of multiple statistical tests.

claim: Kenyon cells are involved in associative learning in Drosophila and other insects.
source: Kenyon cells are involved in associative learning in Drosophila and other insects (Heisenberg, 2003; Aso et al., 2014; Eichler et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Other studies have suggested that certain connections (specifically from antennal lobe projection neurons to Kenyon cells) are random.
source: Other studies have suggested that certain connections (specifically from antennal lobe projection neurons to Kenyon cells) are random (Caron et al., 2013; Eichler et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The marked lack of symmetry observed specifically in the Kenyon cells could be the result of their uniquely non-stereotyped patterns of connectivity in this nervous system.
source: The marked lack of symmetry we observed specifically in the Kenyon cells in the current study could be the result of these features, which suggest their uniquely non-stereotyped patterns of connectivity in this nervous system.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation connecting the observed results to known properties of Kenyon cells.

claim: For either thresholding scheme (synapse count or input proportion), the p-value for each test generally increased as a function of the threshold.
source: We observed that for either thresholding scheme (synapse count or input proportion), the p-value for each test generally increased as a function of the threshold – in other words, the left and right hemisphere networks became less significantly different (under the definitions of 'different' we have presented here) as the edge weight threshold increased.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: The left and right hemisphere networks became less significantly different as the edge weight threshold increased.
source: We observed that for either thresholding scheme (synapse count or input proportion), the p-value for each test generally increased as a function of the threshold – in other words, the left and right hemisphere networks became less significantly different (under the definitions of 'different' we have presented here) as the edge weight threshold increased.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Previous works have shown that higher-weight edges are more likely to have that corresponding edge present on the other side of the nervous system.
source: Previous works have shown that higher-weight edges are more likely to have that corresponding edge present on the other side of the nervous system (Gerhard et al., 2017; Ohyama et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: When thresholding based on synapse counts, the majority (~60%) of the edges of the networks need to be removed for the density-adjusted group connection test to yield non-significant p-values.
source: We found that when thresholding based on synapse counts, the majority (~60%) of the edges of the networks need to be removed for any test (in this case the density-adjusted group connection test) to yield non-significant p-values.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: For thresholds based on input proportion, the density-adjusted group connection test yielded a p-value greater than 0.05 after removing only the weakest ~20% of edges.
source: Conversely, for the thresholds based on input proportion, the density-adjusted group connection test yielded a p-value greater than 0.05 after removing only the weakest ~20% of edges.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: When considering only the strongest ~60% of edges in terms of input proportion, even the density test had a high p-value (>0.05).
source: Strikingly, we observed that when considering only the strongest ~60% of edges in terms of input proportion, even the density test had a high p-value (>0.05), while for the synapse-based thresholds we examined, this never occurred.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Gerhard et al., 2017, observed that while the number of synapses from the mdIV cell type onto various nerve cord local neurons can grow ~3- to 10-fold from L1 to L3, the proportion of that downstream neuron's input stays relatively conserved.
source: Gerhard et al., 2017, compared the connectivity of select neurons in the nerve cord between L1 and L3 stages of the larva. They observed that while the number of synapses from the mdIV cell type onto various nerve cord local neurons can grow ~3- to 10-fold from L1 to L3, the proportion of that downstream neuron's input stays relatively conserved.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Gerhard et al., 2017, suggested that perhaps the nervous system evolved to keep the input proportion parameter constant as the organism develops.

claim: The left and right hemispheres may appear significantly different when considering all observed connections, but the networks formed by only the strongest edges (especially in terms of input proportion) are not significantly different between the hemispheres.
source: Here, we provide further evidence based on the entire brain of the Drosophila larva that while the left and right hemispheres may appear significantly different when considering all observed connections, the networks formed by only the strongest edges (especially in terms of input proportion) are not significantly different between the hemispheres when viewed through the lens of the models considered in this work.
evidence: The claim is based on the combined results of the thresholding experiments.

claim: This work formally states several notions of bilateral symmetry for connectomes as statistical hypotheses.
source: Motivated by the discussion above, in this work we make three major contributions: (1) we formally state several notions of bilateral symmetry for connectomes as statistical hypotheses, (2) we present test procedures for each of these hypotheses of bilateral symmetry, and (3) we demonstrate the utility of these tests for understanding the significance and nature of bilateral symmetry/asymmetry in the brain of a D. melanogaster larva.
